teaching.causalExplanation: One mole of atoms of any element has a mass in grams equal to its relative atomic mass. Carbon's relative atomic mass is twelve point zero one, so one mole of carbon atoms has a mass of twelve point zero one grams. Magnesium's is twenty-four point three one, so one mole of magnesium atoms is twenty-four point three one grams. Each pile holds the same number of atoms, six point zero two two times ten to the twenty-three. Why does that work? Relative atomic masses compare atoms. A magnesium atom is about twice as heavy as a carbon atom. So if two piles hold the same number of atoms, the magnesium pile must be about twice as heavy too. The mole's number was chosen so the carbon pile comes out at about twelve grams, and then every other element follows on the same scale. So the molar mass of a substance is the mass of one mole of it. Its symbol is M M, and its unit is grams per mole, because it tells you how many grams each mole weighs. For the atoms of an element, take the relative atomic mass from the periodic table and add grams per mole. In this course, use the values on the HSC data sheet, like hydrogen, one point zero zero eight, and oxygen, sixteen point zero zero. Notice the difference from Module one. A relative atomic mass has no unit, but a molar mass does, grams per mole.
